function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
**Java** is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language that was originally developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle) and released in 1995. It’s designed to be:

| Feature | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Platform‑independent** | “Write once, run anywhere” – Java programs compile to bytecode that runs on any device with a Java Virtual Machine (JVM). |
| **Object‑oriented** | Everything is an object (except primitives), encouraging modular, reusable code. |
| **Strongly typed** | Types are checked at compile time, reducing runtime errors. |
| **Garbage‑collected** | Automatic memory management frees developers from manual memory deallocation. |
| **Secure** | JVM sandboxing, bytecode verification, and a robust security manager help protect against malicious code. |
| **Concurrent** | Built‑in support for multithreading and synchronization. |

---

### Quick History

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| 1991 | Sun Microsystems founded. |
| 1995 | Java 1.0 released – “Write once, run anywhere.” |
| 1998 | Java 2 (J2SE) introduces Swing, JDBC, and more. |
| 2004 | Java 5 (J2SE 5.0) adds generics, annotations, enums, and the enhanced `for` loop. |
| 2011 | Oracle acquires Sun Microsystems. |
| 2014 | Java 8 introduces lambda expressions, the Stream API, and the new Date/Time API. |
| 2017 | Java 9 introduces the module system (Project Jigsaw). |
| 2020 | Java 14–17 are LTS (Long‑Term Support) releases. |
| 2023 | Java 21 is the latest LTS release. |

---

### Typical Use Cases

| Domain | Why Java? |
|--------|-----------|
| **Enterprise applications** | Robust, scalable, and supported by mature frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE). |
| **Android apps** | Android SDK uses Java (or Kotlin, which interoperates with Java). |
| **Web servers & microservices** | High performance, strong concurrency, and a huge ecosystem of libraries. |
| **Big data & analytics** | Hadoop, Spark, Flink, and other big‑data tools are Java‑based. |
| **Embedded systems** | Java ME (Micro Edition) for IoT devices. |
| **Desktop GUIs** | Swing, JavaFX for cross‑platform desktop apps. |

---

### A Minimal Java Program

```java
// HelloWorld.java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, world!");
    }
}
```

Compile and run:

```bash
javac HelloWorld.java   # compiles to HelloWorld.class (bytecode)
java HelloWorld         # runs on the JVM
```

---

### Common Misconceptions

| Misconception | Reality |
|---------------|---------|
| **Java = JavaScript** | Completely unrelated languages; JavaScript is a scripting language for browsers. |
| **Java is slow** | Modern JVMs use Just‑In‑Time (JIT) compilation and advanced optimizations; Java can be as fast as native code for many workloads. |
| **Java is only for big enterprises** | It’s also popular for small projects, hobbyist coding, and teaching programming fundamentals. |

---

### Getting Started

1. **Install the JDK** (Java Development Kit) – e.g., OpenJDK 21 or Oracle JDK.
2. **Choose an IDE** – IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, or VS Code with Java extensions.
3. **Learn the basics** – syntax, data types, control flow, OOP concepts.
4. **Explore frameworks** – Spring Boot for web services, Hibernate for ORM, etc.

---

### Resources

| Resource | Type | Link |
|----------|------|------|
| Official Java Tutorials | Documentation | https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ |
| Java SE Documentation | API docs | https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/ |
| OpenJDK | Open source JDK | https://openjdk.org/ |
| Spring Boot | Web framework | https://spring.io/projects/spring-boot |
| Java Design Patterns | Patterns & best practices | https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/java |

---

**Bottom line:** Java is a versatile, mature language that powers everything from mobile apps to enterprise servers, thanks to its platform independence, strong typing, and rich ecosystem. Whether you’re building a small utility or a large distributed system, Java provides the tools and community support to get the job done.
